content:
Sharing this update with the community, because the attack was pretty widespread, and to share that the maintainer team is aware of it, but the null hypothesis is that a typical mathlib user shouldn't be affected, as the attack happened within the python ecosystem.

TL;DR: A supply chain attack on the litellm Python package (March 24, 2026) performs a wide exfiltration of all credentials stored in a compromised machine. No compromise of Mathlib infrastructure has been identified, and we are surveying the maintainer team to check for any personal exposure.

The malicious versions were live for approximately 3 hours before PyPI removed them. If you do not use AI coding tools, you are very unlikely to be affected. If you do, see the checks you can perform below.

What happened?

On March 24, 2026, attackers published malicious versions of litellm (versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8) to PyPI, the Python package repository. LiteLLM is a Python library used by AI coding tools and developers to talk to LLM APIs (Claude, GPT, Gemini, etc.) from a single interface.

The attack was part of a larger supply chain compromise: more details can be found here.

Anyone who ran pip install litellm during that window and received version 1.82.7 or 1.82.8 may have had credentials exfiltrated — including API keys, SSH keys, and cloud service credentials. The payload executed automatically on Python startup, so simply having the package installed was sufficient.

Exposure for Mathlib

Mathlib's CI does not use litellm, and all our GitHub Actions are SHA-pinned which protects the pipeline itself from the attack vector that affected Trivy (part of the attack chain that compromised litellm).

We are surveying the maintainer team (with access to mathlib resources) to assess whether anyone has a potentially compromised installation, and will take further action as needed.

Are you personally affected?

You are unaffected if you haven't used Python-based AI tools during the attack window.

LiteLLM is a Python library that provides a unified interface for calling many different LLM APIs (Claude, GPT, Gemini, etc.) with a single consistent function. It's popular with developers building LLM-powered applications, and several AI coding tools use it internally as a dependency.

For the mathlib community, the realistic ways someone would have it are:

  • Installing it directly to experiment with or build LLM-powered tools
  • Other Python LLM frameworks (LangChain, etc.) that pull it in as a dependency
  • Using https://aider.chat/ a popular terminal-based AI coding assistant that depends on litellm

To check, run the following in your terminal:

pip show litellm (or python3 -m pip show litellm)

For a more thorough check that covers all Python environments on your machine (macOS/Linux):

find ~ -name "METADATA" -path "*/litellm*" 2>/dev/null

If neither command finds anything, you are likely not affected. Also see https://snyk.io/articles/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm/#detection-are-you-affected for some additional checks you can perform.

If you find version 1.82.7 or 1.82.8, check remediation steps here, and rotate any credentials accessible on your machine during March 24: API keys (Claude, OpenAI, etc.), SSH keys, GitHub personal access tokens, cloud credentials

For more technical details, see:
- https://snyk.io/articles/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm
- https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/.

Tacking on another PSA on top of this one: There was another big supply chain attack in NPM/Axios yesterday/today. If you performed npm update in the last 24 hours, please check whether you are affected: https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan
